To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the soil bacterial community structure and the number of biodegradation genes are different in soils contaminated by hydrocarbons, in soils from anthropogenic origin, as well as in soils from protected wild-life park areas.

soil bacterial communities from urban and hydrocarbon- contaminated soils differ from agricultural and protected wild-life soil in terms of their structure and the number of dioxygenase genes, which are crucial for biodegrading aromatic hydrocarbons.

the composition of the bacterial metabiomes in the soils studied was different, and that this was related to the number of genes encoding enzymes responsible for the biodegradation processes of aromatic hydrocarbons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of soil bacteria and the determination of genes responsible for biodegradation of hydrocarbons.
the identification of the bacterial population in soils of different origin.

the determination of the structure of the soil bacterial community, the level of genes responsible for biodegradation of mono- and polyaromatic hydrocarbons and the level of genes involved in the degradation of polycyclic aromatic compounds in soils of different origin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
soil bacterial community structure and the presence of dioxygenase genes responsible for biodegradation of hydrocarbons are affected by the type of soil and anthropogenic pressure.

the composition and diversity of soil metabiome as well as the level of genes crucial for the degradation of aromatic hydrocarbons depend on the type of soil, its origin and degree of anthropogenic impact.
the composition and biodiversity of the studied soil metabiome is influenced by the origin of the soil and its contamination level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
soil bacterial communities are characterized by a high diversity and the level of genes responsible for biodegradation of aromatic hydrocarbons depends on the soil type.
the soil bacterial metabiome is a complex system, which is affected by many factors.

the bacterial communities of soils contaminated with hydrocarbons and urban soils are characterized by a lower diversity of bacterial communities, which are dominated by Gammaproteobacterium and contain more genes responsible for the degradation of aromatic compounds than the bacterial communities in soils of agricultural and forest origin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the composition of the soil metabome is not a good indicator of biodegradation potential of soil.
the composition of soil metabiomes is a complex process, and it is necessary to conduct more studies to determine the relationship between bacterial population structure and biodegradation potential.

the composition of bacterial communities in the soil of different origin is different, and the number of dioxygenases is also different, and the level of dioxygenases in the soil of protected areas is lower than in the case of urbanized and contaminated soils.
